segments.english: §16. You who objected to me and said, "Who gave you permission to inquire into and investigate their words?" I am greatly astonished at these words of yours? Was the Torah given to be read in like a chirping bird, or like a bellowing beast that does not know what it is saying? Is not one who does so called a wicked and crafty person, as we learn in Sotah (folio 22): "Ulla said: this is one who read and studied and did not serve the Torah scholars. Rabbi Eliezer said: this one is an unlearned person. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said: this one is an ignoramus. Rabbi Yannai said: this one is a Kuthean. Rabbi Acha bar Yaakov said: this one is a Magian. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said: it stands to reason like Rav Acha bar Yaakov, as people say, 'a Magian's rtin and does not know what rtin is'; a tanna taught, and did not know what he taught." Thus far. And according to your words, the affairs of the body and commercial letters, which are among the affairs of bodily life, are preferable to the affairs of the Torah, which are the life of the soul, through which we merit the life of the world to come, and through them greet the face of our God, our King? For if they bring you two letters of commerce that contradict each other, you pay attention to them, to understand, so that you do not lose, and do not accept them on a craftsman's faith! And in the Torah, which is the life of the soul, would you accept what contradicts your faith, for a craftsman's faith, whether good or bad, without understanding? Is not the main business of the Torah to know and to understand its commandments and statutes! And King David, peace be upon him, said, pleading before the Holy One, blessed be He, "Give me understanding, that I may learn Your commandments." And he said further: "Teach me good judgment and knowledge, for I have trusted in Your commandments." And this is an a fortiori argument: if in the other commandments of the Torah one needs a heart to understand, lest he err by permitting the forbidden, or even by forbidding the permitted, and as our Sages of blessed memory said: Be careful in study, for the error of study counts as wilful sin? how much more so in the commandment of knowing the Name, may He be blessed, and His unity, in accordance with truth and justice, which the Name, may He be blessed, commanded us in the Torah, as it is written: "Know this day, and take it to your heart: that the LORD is God in heaven above, and on the earth below; there is no other." And King David, peace be upon him, charged his son, saying: "Know the God of your father and serve Him." And the prophet Jeremiah proclaims, saying: "Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, let not the strong man glory in his strength, let not the rich man glory in his riches; but in this let him who glories glory, that he has understanding and knows Me, that I am the LORD who performs His kindness, etc." All the more so that we need to know whom we serve.
segments.literal: 16 - you who objected to me and said: who gave you permission to inquire and to investigate after their words? Astonished I greatly at your words, these? Is it indeed that the Torah was given to be read in it, like a bird that chirps, or like a beast that bellows and does not know what it is saying? Is it not that one who does so is called wicked, crafty, as we learn in Sotah folio 22: Ulla said: this is one who read and studied and not served the Torah scholars. Rabbi Eliezer said: this one is people of the land. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said: behold this one an ignoramus. Rabbi Yannai said: this one is a Kuthean. Rabbi Acha bar Yaakov said: this one is a Magian. Said Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: it stands to reason like Rav Acha bar Yaakov, as they say, people: rtin of a Magian, and not knows what rtin; taught a tanna and not knows what he taught. Thus far. And according to your words the affairs of the body, and letters of commerce which are of the affairs of life of the bodies, are preferable to the affair of the Torah which are life of the soul, in which we merit to the life of the world, the coming, and we greet with them the face of our God, our King? For if they bring to you two letters of commerce which contradict one the other, you give heart to them, to understand so that not you lose, and not you accept them with faith of a craftsman! And in the Torah which is life of the soul, will you accept the contradicting your faith, for faith of a craftsman whether good or bad without understanding? Is it not the main business of the Torah to know and to understand its commandments and its statutes! And David the king, peace on him, said, pleading before the Holy One, blessed be He: make me understand and that I learn Your commandments. And said further: good judgment and knowledge teach me, for in Your commandments I trusted. Light and heavy this is: if in the rest of commandments of the Torah needs a heart to understand, lest he err by permitting - the forbidden, or even by forbidding - the permitted, and as the saying of our Sages of blessed memory: be careful in study, that the error of study counts as wilful sin? in the commandment of knowing the Name, may He be blessed, and His unity, according to the mouth of truth and justice which commanded us the Name in the Torah, as it is written: and know this day and take to your heart that the LORD He is God in heaven above and on the earth below there is no other. And David the king, peace on him, charged his son saying: know - the God of your father and serve Him. And the prophet Jeremiah proclaims saying: let not the wise glory in his wisdom, and let not the strong glory in his strength, let not the rich glory in his riches; but only in this let glory the one who glories, has understanding and knows Me, that I the LORD who performs His kindness, etc. For one how much and how much, that we need to know - whom we serve.
segments.note: The paragraph is the author's reply to an objector (§16). The Sotah 22 passage is quoted at length; its Aramaic words are translated by sense. The kal va-chomer in the middle has an elided apodosis, supplied as 'how much more so'. Ulla's saying takes the main clause 'this is'. The closing ע״כ is 'Thus far', outside the quotation mark. The author's rtin is left untranslated, since no sense is given in the text.

grammar: ואשר טענת עלי ואמרת: the author addresses an objector in the second person ('you'), and the English keeps that voice to the end of the objection.
The Sotah 22 quotation is Talmudic; its proverb 'דאמרי אינשי רטין מגושא' and the words מסתברא, תני תנא are Bavli Aramaic, translated by sense.
ומה בשאר מצות של תורה צריך לב להבין: a kal va-chomer. The protasis is complete; the apodosis ('how much more so') is elided and is supplied in the English.
Deut 4:39 and Ps 119:66 and 119:73 are quoted with the Hebrew imperatives and perfects rendered in the sense of the verse ('Know'; 'Teach me'; 'Give me understanding').
אל יתהלל is a negative jussive, 'let not ... glory'; כי אם בזאת יתהלל is the same verb, 'but in this let ... glory', and the English keeps the parallel.
apparatus: Wikisource additions (Q2): translated as base text, flagged here until the 1931 scan is collated.
Section number: the opening label טז) is §16.
Sotah 22: the author writes 'דף כב.' with no a or b; nothing is added.
The author writes רב in 'כרב אחא בר יעקב' and ר׳ in 'ר׳ אחא בר יעקב'; the same name appears to be meant.
Deut 4:39: the author quotes 'וידעת היום והשבות אל לבבך כי ה׳ הוא האלהים בשמים ממעל ועל הארץ מתחת אין עוד' in full.
1 Chron 28:9: the author quotes 'דע את אלהי אביך ועבדהו' and stops there; the verse continues 'בלבב שלם', and nothing is added.
Ps 119:73: 'הבינני ואלמדה מצותיך'. Ps 119:66: 'טוב טעם ודעת למדני כי במצותיך האמנתי'.
Jer 9:22–23: the author writes 'עושה חסדו' where the verse reads 'עושה חסד משפט וצדקה בארץ'; the author's wording is followed and 'וכו׳' keeps the cut.
context: Magian (אמגוש): a member of the Magi, the priestly class of the Persian religion (Zoroastrianism).
Kuthean (כותי): the Talmud's term for a Samaritan.
